analysis.one_liner: Toughens mine safety enforcement, raises penalties for safety violations, and protects workers who report hazards.
analysis.headline: The mine and workplace safety bill was referred to the Senate health committee in January 2011 and never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: After a string of coal mine disasters, this bill would have overhauled federal mine safety law: stricter inspections, bigger fines and prison terms for operators whose violations kill miners, an independent investigation of any disaster with three or more deaths, a public database of each mine's safety record, and pay for miners idled by safety shutdowns. It also extended stronger worker protections and penalties to workplaces covered by OSHA generally. The Senate never acted on it.
analysis.who_benefits: Coal miners and their families, and workers in OSHA-covered workplaces generally. Miners would gain the right to refuse dangerous work without retaliation, full pay while a safety order idles the mine, private interviews with investigators without the operator present, and access to a public database of every mine's safety record [S2]. Families of miners trapped in accidents could designate a representative to participate in inspections [S3]. Workers killed or hurt by a knowing employer violation would gain new victim rights and their employers would face far higher civil and criminal penalties [S2].

how_it_helps.text: Miners idled by a safety withdrawal order would be paid at their regular rate for the entire idled period; current law pays only the rest of the shift plus up to four hours [S2].

A miner who refuses dangerous work based on a good-faith, reasonable belief of a safety hazard would be protected from firing or discrimination, and retaliation would carry civil penalties and up to 10 years' imprisonment [S3].

Any accident killing three or more miners would trigger an independent investigation by a panel appointed by the Department of Health and Human Services, with members free of conflicts of interest and findings published publicly [S3].
Investigators could question workers privately without the operator or its attorneys present, and the Secretary could subpoena witnesses and records [S3].

Mines with recurring violations or accidents would face mandatory shutdowns, doubled penalties, extra inspections paid through operator fees, and doubled fines if they failed performance benchmarks [S3].

Maximum civil penalties for significant and substantial violations would rise to $150,000 per violation, and criminal fines for knowing violations causing death would rise from $250,000 to $1,000,000, with prison terms up to five years instead of one [S3].
Corporate officers and directors who knowingly authorized a violation would face the same penalties as the operator [S3].

Underground coal mines would have to raise the incombustible content of rock dust from 65% to 80% to reduce explosion risk, install atmospheric monitoring systems, and give every miner a pre-shift briefing on current mine conditions [S3].
OSHA-covered employers nationwide would face raised civil penalties, new criminal penalties for knowing violations causing serious bodily harm, and victims' rights in enforcement proceedings [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Coal mine operators, who would bear higher civil and criminal penalties, fees for extra inspections and certification, the cost of new dust monitoring and atmospheric monitoring equipment, and full wages for miners idled by safety shutdowns [S3]. Employers across the economy covered by OSHA would face higher civil penalties and new criminal exposure for knowing violations causing death or serious injury [S2].
analysis.who_pays_short: Coal mine operators and OSHA-covered employers

drawbacks.text: The compliance burden falls hardest on smaller operators: fees for extra inspections and personnel certification, new monitoring equipment, and full pay for all miners during any withdrawal order, which can extend for weeks [S3].

Placing a mine in 'pattern status' immediately withdraws all personnel from the mine, which could shut a working mine for an extended period before remediation is complete, with costs to operators and local mining communities [S3].

The bill attaches personal civil and criminal liability to individual officers and directors who knowingly authorize violations, a significant expansion of individual exposure that companies and executives objected to in the broader mine-safety debate [S3].
Raising OSHA criminal penalties and creating penalties for violations causing serious bodily harm extends these costs and liabilities to employers in every industry, not just mining [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits are concrete and tied to a known failure pattern: the bill's provisions on independent investigations, pattern-of-violations shutdowns, dust standards, and whistleblower protection respond directly to the circumstances of the 2010 Upper Big Branch disaster, where 29 miners died and miners had reported being unable to speak freely with investigators [S2]. The costs — compliance spending, fees, and shutdown risk for operators, and broader OSHA penalties for employers — are real but are the intended price of enforcement. The main design tension is that withdrawal orders in pattern status impose sudden, open-ended shutdown costs, which supporters would call the point and critics would call disproportionate.

outcome.mechanism: It was read twice and referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee never held a hearing or vote on it, so it died when the 112th Congress ended [S5].

narrative.text: Senator John D. Rockefeller IV introduced the bill on January 25, 2011, joined by Senators Harkin, Murray, and Manchin as original cosponsors [S1].

The bill was named for Senator Robert C. Byrd of West Virginia, and followed the April 2010 Upper Big Branch mine explosion that killed 29 miners; its provisions on independent investigations, pre-shift condition briefings, and private miner interviews respond to findings from that disaster [S2].
The Senate's only action was to read the bill twice and refer it to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions on January 25, 2011 [S5].
The action record shows no further activity — no hearings, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor vote — through the end of the 112th Congress on January 3, 2013 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Coal mine operators and other employers gained because none of the higher penalties, shutdown powers, or worker protections ever took effect, leaving enforcement under the 1977 mine safety law unchanged.

sides.party_line_note: All four sponsors were Senate Democrats and no Republican cosponsored the bill; it never advanced far enough for any roll-call vote, so the party split shows only in sponsorship [S4].

industries.note: The bill would subject operators to much higher civil and criminal penalties, personal liability for executives, fees, mandatory shutdowns for repeat violators, full pay for idled miners, and costly new dust and monitoring standards. Operators' savings from avoiding these costs come at the price of continued safety risk borne by miners.
Mandates for atmospheric monitoring systems and direct-reading dust monitors would create a market for detection and monitoring equipment installed in underground coal mines.

Title VII would raise civil penalties, add criminal penalties for knowing violations causing death or serious harm, and create victims' rights in OSHA enforcement. Better enforcement protects workers, but compliance and penalty costs would spread across every covered industry.
The bill would raise federal grants to states to $20 million per year and fund state miner certification programs.
